title: Theta is not linear: use the decay schedule to roll short options early
summary: Theta is the cost of convexity. It is not linear: a weekly option decays slowly at first and most decay comes at the end, with about 37% on the last day. A seller expects about 25% after three days. If a sold call is already up 50-70% because the stock fell, the speaker rolls it to earn more than the week's plan.

steps.caption: A sold at-the-money weekly call on a $100 stock.
At expiry the short call keeps the full premium if the stock stays below $100.
Decay is slow at first: after three of seven days, only about 25% of the premium is gone.
Most decay comes at the end: about 37% of it on the last day.
If the stock dips and the call is up 50-70% after three days, you are ahead of schedule: roll it.
Short calls carry open-ended risk if the stock rallies hard.
The surface shows P&L across price and time: the drop in value speeds up near expiry.

takeaways: Theta is the price of convexity and it is not linear.
Short-dated options decay most in the last days.
When a sale is ahead of its theta schedule, roll to capture more.
caveats: The decay percentages come from the speaker's table and depend on volatility and strike.
A naked short call has undefined risk; owner rules require defined risk.
